definition: According to what people claim, even though it has not been proven.
example: The old lighthouse is allegedly haunted, yet no visitor has ever captured a single strange photo.
nuance: Allegedly stresses that a claim is still unproven, while reportedly only says the information was passed along by someone.
prompt: A neighbor blames a dog for the ruined flower bed, but no one saw what happened.
options: The dog allegedly dug up the tulips, but nobody saw it.
I allegedly watched the dog dig up the tulips with my own two eyes this morning.
The dog dug allegedly, flinging dirt quickly across the whole lawn.
Security footage clearly proves that the dog allegedly dug up the tulips.
reasons: The claim against the dog is unconfirmed, which is exactly when this word fits.
An eyewitness speaking about what they saw themselves has no reason to signal doubt.
The word marks a claim as unproven; it cannot describe the manner of an action.
Once video proves something, it is no longer just a claim, so the hedge contradicts the proof.

practice.prompt: Customers hear a rumor that a small bakery's pie won a county contest.
options: The baker sliced the pie so allegedly that every single piece came out perfectly even.
I baked this pie myself this morning, so I know it allegedly contains three cups of cherries.
The judges' official results confirm that the pie allegedly took first place.
The bakery's cherry pie allegedly won a county prize, but I can't find any record of it.
reasons: This treats the word like carefully, but it qualifies a claim rather than describing skill.
The baker has direct knowledge of the recipe, so casting doubt on it makes no sense.
Official confirmation removes the doubt that the word is meant to express.
The prize is talked about but not verified, so signaling an unproven claim is right.
